claim: The glycyl radical enzyme (GRE) superfamily utilizes a glycyl radical cofactor to catalyze difficult chemical reactions in a variety of anaerobic microbial metabolic pathways.
source: The glycyl radical enzyme (GRE) superfamily utilizes a glycyl radical cofactor to catalyze difficult chemical reactions in a variety of anaerobic microbial metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about GRE superfamily function.

claim: A GRE, trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline (Hyp) dehydratase (HypD), catalyzes the dehydration of Hyp to (S)-Δ1-pyrroline-5-carboxylic acid (P5C).
source: Recently, a GRE, trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline (Hyp) dehydratase (HypD), was discovered that catalyzes the dehydration of Hyp to (S)-Δ1-pyrroline-5-carboxylic acid (P5C).
evidence: This statement references a recent discovery and is supported by citation to prior work (Levin et al., 2017).

claim: HypD is abundant in the human gut microbiome.
source: This enzyme is abundant in the human gut microbiome and also present in prominent bacterial pathogens.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analyses mentioned later in the text (Levin et al., 2017).

claim: HypD is present in prominent bacterial pathogens.
source: This enzyme is abundant in the human gut microbiome and also present in prominent bacterial pathogens.
evidence: This is supported by the text mentioning C. difficile as a pathogen containing HypD.

claim: The crystal structure of HypD from Clostridioides difficile with Hyp bound in the active site has been solved.
source: Here, we have solved the crystal structure of HypD from the pathogen Clostridioides difficile with Hyp bound in the active site.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by crystallographic data presented in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Biochemical studies have led to the identification of key catalytic residues in HypD.
source: Biochemical studies have led to the identification of key catalytic residues and have provided insight into the radical mechanism of Hyp dehydration.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments and activity assays presented in Figures 5 and Table 2.

claim: Biochemical studies have provided insight into the radical mechanism of Hyp dehydration.
source: Biochemical studies have led to the identification of key catalytic residues and have provided insight into the radical mechanism of Hyp dehydration.
evidence: This is supported by deuterium labeling experiments shown in Figure 6 and mechanistic proposals in Figure 7.

claim: The human gastrointestinal tract has an estimated 10^11 bacterial cells per gram.
source: The most densely populated microbial environment among human body sites is the gastrointestinal (GI) tract with an estimated 1011 bacterial cells per gram (Tropini et al., 2017; Sender et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The GI tract is largely anoxic.
source: Due to the largely anoxic nature of the GI tract, this body site is inhabited by facultative and obligate anaerobes that perform a wide variety of challenging chemical transformations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GI tract environment.

claim: Recent studies suggest correlations between changes in gut microbiome composition and diseases such as metabolic disorders, cardiovascular diseases, autoimmune diseases, and neurological disorders.
source: Recent studies suggest correlations between changes in gut microbiome composition and diseases, such as metabolic disorders, cardiovascular diseases, autoimmune diseases, and neurological disorders (Sharon et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hyp is an abundant nutrient in the GI tract.
source: Hyp is an abundant nutrient in the GI tract.
evidence: This is supported by information about Hyp being generated from collagen and present in the human diet.

claim: Hyp is generated from hydroxylation of Pro residues within proteins like collagen.
source: Generated from hydroxylation of Pro residues within proteins like collagen (Gorres and Raines, 2010), this nonproteinogenic amino acid represents the most abundant post-translational modification in mammals and is also found in the human diet (Vázquez‐Ortíz et al., 2004; Verbeken et al., 2003; Valiente et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hyp represents the most abundant post-translational modification in mammals.
source: Generated from hydroxylation of Pro residues within proteins like collagen (Gorres and Raines, 2010), this nonproteinogenic amino acid represents the most abundant post-translational modification in mammals and is also found in the human diet (Vázquez‐Ortíz et al., 2004; Verbeken et al., 2003; Valiente et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hyp is found in the human diet.
source: Generated from hydroxylation of Pro residues within proteins like collagen (Gorres and Raines, 2010), this nonproteinogenic amino acid represents the most abundant post-translational modification in mammals and is also found in the human diet (Vázquez‐Ortíz et al., 2004; Verbeken et al., 2003; Valiente et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bioinformatic analyses of metagenomes indicate HypD is one of the most abundant GREs in the healthy human gut microbiome.
source: Bioinformatic analyses of metagenomes indicate HypD is one of the most abundant GREs in the healthy human gut microbiome, thus suggesting it plays an important role in many bacteria (Levin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published bioinformatic analysis.

claim: P5C is a central metabolite in amino acid biosynthetic pathways.
source: P5C is a central metabolite in amino acid biosynthetic pathways, providing a source of building blocks for protein synthesis and/or of carbon and nitrogen (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In gut Clostridiales, Hyp enables amino acid fermentation, also known as Stickland fermentation.
source: In gut Clostridiales, Hyp enables amino acid fermentation, also known as Stickland fermentation (Stickland, 1934).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stickland's work.

claim: The formation of Pro as a downstream metabolite during Hyp fermentation by Clostridiales results in the chemical reversal of the post-translational modification of Pro to Hyp.
source: The formation of Pro as a downstream metabolite during Hyp fermentation by Clostridiales results in the chemical reversal of the post-translational modification of Pro to Hyp, which was not previously thought to occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic pathway and represents a novel finding.

claim: The chemical reversal of the post-translational modification of Pro to Hyp was not previously thought to occur.
source: The formation of Pro as a downstream metabolite during Hyp fermentation by Clostridiales results in the chemical reversal of the post-translational modification of Pro to Hyp, which was not previously thought to occur.
evidence: This represents a novel insight from the work.

claim: HypD is found in Clostridioides difficile.
source: In addition to commensal Clostridiales, HypD is found in the prominent antibiotic-resistant opportunistic pathogen Clostridioides difficile, formerly known as Clostridium difficile.
evidence: This is supported by genomic data and the structural work presented in this manuscript.

claim: In 2015, C. difficile was responsible for approximately 500,000 infections and 29,000 deaths.
source: In 2015, C. difficile was responsible for approximately 500,000 infections and 29,000 deaths, making this pathogen a major health concern (Leffler and Lamont, 2015; Lessa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: HypD could be a promising antibiotic target for C. difficile and other pathogens.
source: As a key metabolic enzyme, with no protein homolog in humans, HypD could be a promising antibiotic target for C. difficile and other pathogens.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on HypD's metabolic importance and absence in humans.

claim: HypD has no protein homolog in humans.
source: As a key metabolic enzyme, with no protein homolog in humans, HypD could be a promising antibiotic target for C. difficile and other pathogens.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and established knowledge that GREs are not found in humans.

claim: All GREs use a glycine-centered radical cofactor for catalysis.
source: All GREs use a glycine-centered radical cofactor for catalysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GRE mechanism.

claim: GREs are activated by a cognate S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet)-dependent activating enzyme (AE), generating a protein-based radical on a conserved Gly residue positioned within the GRE active site.
source: Briefly, these enzymes are activated by a cognate S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet)-dependent activating enzyme (AE), generating a protein-based radical on a conserved Gly residue positioned within the GRE active site (Figure 1B; Conradt et al., 1984).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GRE activation mechanism, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The glycyl radical in GREs generates a catalytically essential thiyl radical on a conserved Cys.
source: The glycyl radical in turn generates a catalytically essential thiyl radical on a conserved Cys, which initiates the chemical transformation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GRE mechanism.

claim: Upon product formation in GREs, the thiyl radical is regenerated and the radical species is returned to the Gly residue for storage.
source: Upon product formation, the thiyl radical is regenerated and the radical species is returned to the Gly residue for storage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GRE catalytic cycle.

claim: HypD is part of the eliminase class of GREs.
source: HypD is part of the eliminase class of GREs, which includes glycerol dehydratase (GD), propanediol dehydratase (PD), choline trimethylamine-lyase (CutC), and the recently identified isethionate sulfite-lyase (IslA) (Backman et al., 2017; O'Brien et al., 2004; LaMattina et al., 2016; Kalnins et al., 2015; Xing et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on GRE classification.

claim: Several eliminases catalyze transformations with reactivities that are also performed by adenosylcobalamin (coenzyme B12)-dependent enzymes.
source: Interestingly, several of the eliminases catalyze transformations with reactivities that are also performed by adenosylcobalamin (coenzyme B12)-dependent enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by examples and citations provided in the text.

claim: Dehydration of 1,2-propanediol and glycerol was first discovered in the 1960s as an activity catalyzed by a B12-dependent propanediol dehydratase.
source: For example, dehydration of 1,2-propanediol and glycerol was first discovered in the 1960s as an activity catalyzed by a B12-dependent propanediol dehydratase (Zagalak et al., 1966; Rétey et al., 1966).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: Choline cleavage by CutC resembles the activity of ethanolamine ammonia-lyase, a B12-dependent enzyme.
source: Additionally, choline cleavage by CutC resembles the activity of ethanolamine ammonia-lyase, a B12-dependent enzyme that catalyzes an analogous C–N bond cleavage of ethanolamine using radical chemistry (Craciun and Balskus, 2012; Mori et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature.

claim: Dehydration of Hyp to P5C does not have precedence in B12 enzymology.
source: In contrast, dehydration of Hyp to P5C does not have precedence in B12 enzymology, nor does the C–S bond cleavage of IslA (Xing et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of B12-dependent enzyme reactions and citation.

claim: The C–S bond cleavage of IslA does not have precedence in B12 enzymology.
source: In contrast, dehydration of Hyp to P5C does not have precedence in B12 enzymology, nor does the C–S bond cleavage of IslA (Xing et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to IslA literature.

claim: The oxidation of a C–N bond that occurs in HypD is unprecedented among GREs.
source: In particular, the oxidation of a C–N bond that occurs in HypD is unprecedented among GREs since all other eliminases catalyze the oxidation of a C–O bond to generate aldehyde products (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison with other GRE eliminases and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All other GRE eliminases catalyze the oxidation of a C–O bond to generate aldehyde products.
source: In particular, the oxidation of a C–N bond that occurs in HypD is unprecedented among GREs since all other eliminases catalyze the oxidation of a C–O bond to generate aldehyde products (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of GRE eliminase mechanisms and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The substrate of HypD is a conformationally constrained pyrrolidine ring lacking a freely rotatable Cα–Cβ bond.
source: Another notable feature of HypD is that its substrate is a conformationally constrained pyrrolidine ring lacking a freely rotatable Cα–Cβ bond (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is based on the chemical structure of Hyp shown in figures.

claim: Among GREs, the enzyme with the most similar substrate to HypD is the class III ribonucleotide reductase (RNR).
source: Among GREs, the enzyme with the most similar substrate is the class III ribonucleotide reductase (RNR), which also acts on a substrate with a 5-membered heterocyclic ring (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of substrate structures shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The reaction of RNR is more similar to that of diol dehydratases than it is to HypD.
source: The reaction of RNR, however, is more similar to that of diol dehydratases than it is to HypD.
evidence: This is based on comparison of reaction mechanisms.

claim: The enzyme-catalyzed reaction most similar to HypD is the dehydration of cytidine triphosphate (CTP) performed by the AdoMet radical enzyme viperin.
source: Perhaps the enzyme-catalyzed reaction most similar to the reaction catalyzed by HypD is the dehydration of the ribose-containing substrate cytidine triphosphate (CTP) performed by the recently characterized AdoMet radical enzyme viperin (Gizzi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on comparison of reaction mechanisms and supported by citation.

claim: Viperin's reaction involves the elimination of a hydroxyl group on the carbon position β to a C–O bond within the 5-membered ring.
source: This reaction is reminiscent of Hyp dehydration because it involves the elimination of a hydroxyl group on the carbon position β to a C–O bond within the 5-membered ring (Gizzi et al., 2018), although it lacks the C–N oxidation catalyzed by HypD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Viperin's reaction lacks the C–N oxidation catalyzed by HypD.
source: This reaction is reminiscent of Hyp dehydration because it involves the elimination of a hydroxyl group on the carbon position β to a C–O bond within the 5-membered ring (Gizzi et al., 2018), although it lacks the C–N oxidation catalyzed by HypD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of reaction mechanisms and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A structure of HypD from C. difficile 70-100-2010 was solved by molecular replacement to 2.05 Å resolution using CutC (PDB: 5FAU) as the search model.
source: A structure of HypD from C. difficile 70-100-2010 was solved by molecular replacement to 2.05 Å resolution using the GRE homolog CutC (PDB: 5FAU) (Bodea et al., 2016) as the search model (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: Electron density resembling glycerol was observed in the active site of HypD during model refinement.
source: During model refinement, we observed electron density resembling glycerol in the active site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron density maps shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glycerol binding in the HypD structure is likely an artifact from the cryoprotectant.
source: Although we believe that glycerol binding is an artifact (glycerol was used as a cryoprotectant), it is not surprising that glycerol is able to bind given HypD's high sequence similarity to GD.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental conditions and sequence similarity.

claim: The Hyp-bound HypD structure was solved to 2.52 Å resolution by molecular replacement using the glycerol-bound HypD structure as the search model.
source: This second HypD structure was solved to 2.52 Å resolution by molecular replacement using the glycerol-bound HypD structure as the search model (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: HypD is dimeric with each monomer consisting of two five-stranded half β-barrels, anti-parallel to one another and surrounded by α-helices.
source: In agreement with all characterized GREs (O'Brien et al., 2004; LaMattina et al., 2016; Kalnins et al., 2015; Xing et al., 2019; Bodea et al., 2016), HypD is dimeric with each monomer consisting of two five-stranded half β-barrels, anti-parallel to one another and surrounded by α-helices (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A and citations to other GRE structures.

claim: The active site of HypD is buried within the center of the barrel.
source: The active site is buried within the center of the barrel, which is thought to protect radical species from being quenched by solvent.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure and is consistent with other GREs.

claim: Burying the active site within the barrel is thought to protect radical species from being quenched by solvent.
source: The active site is buried within the center of the barrel, which is thought to protect radical species from being quenched by solvent.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the structural feature.

claim: Two loops essential for catalysis are juxtaposed in the active site: the Gly loop and the Cys loop.
source: Two loops essential for catalysis are juxtaposed in the active site: the Gly loop and the Cys loop (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Gly loop contains the conserved Gly residue (Gly765 in HypD).
source: The Gly loop contains the conserved Gly residue (Gly765 in HypD) and is part of the C-terminal glycyl radical domain that is found in all GREs (Backman et al., 2017) whereas the neighboring Cys loop contains the catalytic Cys434 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure and citation.

claim: The Cys loop contains the catalytic Cys434.
source: The Gly loop contains the conserved Gly residue (Gly765 in HypD) and is part of the C-terminal glycyl radical domain that is found in all GREs (Backman et al., 2017) whereas the neighboring Cys loop contains the catalytic Cys434 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: Gly765 is located 3.9 Å from Cys434.
source: Gly765 is located 3.9 Å from Cys434 (Figure 2C), consistent with radical transfer from Gly765 to Cys434 to generate a transient thiyl radical for initiation of catalysis on substrate.
evidence: This is a measurement from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The distance between Gly765 and Cys434 is consistent with radical transfer from Gly765 to Cys434.
source: Gly765 is located 3.9 Å from Cys434 (Figure 2C), consistent with radical transfer from Gly765 to Cys434 to generate a transient thiyl radical for initiation of catalysis on substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural distance and knowledge of GRE mechanism.

claim: Electron density maps are best fit by Hyp in a Cγ-exo configuration.
source: To investigate whether Hyp binds to HypD in the Cγ-exo or Cγ-endo pucker state (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), we modeled and refined both configurations of Hyp into the electron density and found that the electron density maps are best fit by a Cγ-exo configuration (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by electron density maps shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Cγ-exo pucker of zwitterionic Hyp is more energetically favorable than the Cγ-endo pucker by 2.7 kcal mol−1.
source: Additionally, we calculated the energies associated with these two configurations of zwitterionic Hyp (see Methods) and found the Cγ-exo pucker to be more energetically favorable than the Cγ-endo pucker by 2.7 kcal mol−1.
evidence: This is based on DFT calculations described in the Methods.

claim: Free Hyp prefers the Cγ-exo pucker.
source: A preference for the Cγ-exo pucker has also been noted for free Hyp (Lesarri et al., 2005) and peptidyl Hyp in the context of collagen structure (Shoulders and Raines, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Peptidyl Hyp in the context of collagen structure prefers the Cγ-exo pucker.
source: A preference for the Cγ-exo pucker has also been noted for free Hyp (Lesarri et al., 2005) and peptidyl Hyp in the context of collagen structure (Shoulders and Raines, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: C5 of Hyp is proposed as the site of hydrogen atom abstraction.
source: The Cγ-exo puckering of the pyrrolidine ring orients C5 of Hyp in closest proximity to Cys434, prompting us to propose C5 as the site of hydrogen atom abstraction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystal structure and proximity measurements.

claim: The distance between C5 of Hyp and the sulfur atom of Cys434 is 3.8 Å.
source: The distance between C5 and the sulfur atom of Cys434 is 3.8 Å (Figure 2C), a typical distance between the site of hydrogen atom abstraction and the catalytic cysteine in other structurally characterized GREs (Backman et al., 2017; Vey et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a measurement from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 3.8 Å is a typical distance between the site of hydrogen atom abstraction and the catalytic cysteine in other structurally characterized GREs.
source: The distance between C5 and the sulfur atom of Cys434 is 3.8 Å (Figure 2C), a typical distance between the site of hydrogen atom abstraction and the catalytic cysteine in other structurally characterized GREs (Backman et al., 2017; Vey et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to other GRE structures.

claim: In the Cγ-exo pucker conformation, the dihedral angle between the amino group and the hydroxyl leaving group of Hyp is 75.8°.
source: We calculate that in the observed Cγ-exo pucker conformation, the dihedral angle between the amino group and the hydroxyl leaving group of Hyp is 75.8°, similar to the dihedral angles (~60°) observed for substrates bound to other GRE eliminases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; O'Brien et al., 2004; LaMattina et al., 2016; Bodea et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a calculation from the crystal structure.

claim: The dihedral angle of 75.8° in Hyp is similar to the dihedral angles (~60°) observed for substrates bound to other GRE eliminases.
source: We calculate that in the observed Cγ-exo pucker conformation, the dihedral angle between the amino group and the hydroxyl leaving group of Hyp is 75.8°, similar to the dihedral angles (~60°) observed for substrates bound to other GRE eliminases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; O'Brien et al., 2004; LaMattina et al., 2016; Bodea et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison with other GRE structures cited and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hyp in the Cγ-endo pucker conformation has a dihedral angle of 165° between the amino group and the hydroxyl leaving group.
source: In contrast, Hyp in the Cγ-endo pucker conformation has a dihedral angle of 165° between the amino group and the hydroxyl leaving group.
evidence: This is a calculation from the modeled structure.

claim: Hyp is positioned in the active site through a series of hydrogen bonds that include: Glu436 of the Cys loop, Asp278 of the β1 strand, Ser334 of a short α-helix between the β2 and β3 strands, Thr645 of β8 strand, and a water molecule that interacts with Asp339 of the β3 strand.
source: Hyp is positioned in the active site through a series of hydrogen bonds that include: Glu436 of the Cys loop, Asp278 of the β1 strand, Ser334 of a short α-helix between the β2 and β3 strands, Thr645 of β8 strand, and a water molecule that interacts with Asp339 of the β3 strand (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hydrophobic contacts may play a role in the positioning of Hyp.
source: In addition, hydrophobic contacts may play a role in the positioning of Hyp (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Cys loop of HypD contains the CXE motif (Cys434-Val435-Glu436) that is conserved among GRE eliminases.
source: The Cys loop of HypD contains the CXE motif (Cys434-Val435-Glu436) that is conserved among GRE eliminases (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C; O'Brien et al., 2004; LaMattina et al., 2016; Xing et al., 2019; Bodea et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison with other GRE structures, supported by citations.

claim: In previous GRE eliminase structures, the Glu of the CXE motif is observed to interact with a hydroxyl group of substrate through a hydrogen bond.
source: In previous GRE eliminase structures, the Glu of the CXE motif is observed to interact with a hydroxyl group of substrate through a hydrogen bond (Figure 3B–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C; O'Brien et al., 2004; LaMattina et al., 2016; Xing et al., 2019; Bodea et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on analysis of other GRE structures cited and shown in figures.

claim: In other GRE eliminases, the Glu of the CXE motif is proposed to deprotonate the substrate's hydroxyl group to form a ketyl radical intermediate.
source: In these cases, the Glu is proposed to deprotonate the substrate's hydroxyl group to form a ketyl radical intermediate that aids in the elimination of a different hydroxyl group (diol dehydratases), trimethylamine (CutC), or sulfite (IslA) (Figure 3; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 3; O'Brien et al., 2004; LaMattina et al., 2016; Xing et al., 2019; Bodea et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on mechanistic proposals for other GRE eliminases, supported by citations.

claim: In HypD, Glu436 is positioned to hydrogen bond with the hydroxyl group of Hyp.
source: In HypD, we also find that Glu436 is positioned to hydrogen bond with the hydroxyl group of Hyp (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In HypD, the Hyp hydroxyl group is the leaving group.
source: However, in HypD, the Hyp hydroxyl group is the leaving group, and therefore it is the leaving group that points toward and interacts with the Glu of the CXE motif rather than pointing away as is the case for the other GRE eliminases.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure and comparison with other GREs.

claim: In HypD, the orientation of the substrate's leaving group with respect to the CXE is reversed compared to other GRE eliminases.
source: Thus, the orientation of the substrate's leaving group with respect to the CXE is reversed and the fate of this hydroxyl group is unique in the HypD-catalyzed reaction.
evidence: This is based on comparison of HypD structure with other GRE eliminase structures.

claim: The fate of the hydroxyl group is unique in the HypD-catalyzed reaction.
source: Thus, the orientation of the substrate's leaving group with respect to the CXE is reversed and the fate of this hydroxyl group is unique in the HypD-catalyzed reaction.
evidence: This is based on mechanistic analysis and comparison with other GREs.

claim: There are no strictly conserved sequences among GRE eliminases outside of the Cys and Gly loop motifs.
source: Outside of the Cys and Gly loop motifs, there are no strictly conserved sequences among GRE eliminases (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The hydroxyl group of Hyp is within hydrogen bonding distance of Asp278.
source: In addition to interacting with Glu436, the hydroxyl group of Hyp is also within hydrogen bonding distance of Asp278 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The amino group of Hyp makes interactions with Asp278 and Asp339, the latter through water.
source: The amino group of Hyp, which must be deprotonated as part of the reaction cycle, makes interactions with Asp278 and Asp339, the latter through water (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Water interactions with Asp339 are present in all active sites of the 8 molecules in the asymmetric unit.
source: Notably, these water interactions are present in all active sites of the 8 molecules in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Asp339 and Asp278 are strictly conserved in HypD but are not conserved in other GRE eliminases.
source: Asp339 and Asp278 are strictly conserved in HypD but are not conserved in other GRE eliminases (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: HypD uses three polar, uncharged residues (Ser334, Thr645, Tyr450) to hydrogen bond to the Hyp carboxylate moiety.
source: Interestingly, HypD uses three polar, uncharged residues (Ser334, Thr645, Tyr450) to hydrogen bond to the Hyp carboxylate moiety (Figure 4B), all of which are conserved in HypD (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4B and sequence alignment.

claim: Ser334, Thr645, and Tyr450 are all conserved in HypD.
source: Interestingly, HypD uses three polar, uncharged residues (Ser334, Thr645, Tyr450) to hydrogen bond to the Hyp carboxylate moiety (Figure 4B), all of which are conserved in HypD (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Ser334 is positioned in the space that is often occupied by a Phe residue in other GRE eliminases.
source: Ser334 is positioned in the space that is often occupied by a Phe residue in other GRE eliminases (Phe333 in GD, Phe389 in CutC, Phe338 in PD, and Phe680 in IslA) (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with other GREs shown in figures.

claim: Arg156 and Lys326 may contribute to charge stabilization of the Hyp carboxylate.
source: Arg156 and Lys326 may contribute to charge stabilization of the Hyp carboxylate, although they do not directly interact with substrate (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HypD has many aromatic residues in its active site.
source: As is the case for other GREs, HypD has many aromatic residues in its active site (Figure 3D–F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F; Backman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in figures and citation.

claim: Phe152, Trp277, and Phe340 are in contact with the substrate in HypD.
source: In HypD, Phe152, Trp277, and Phe340 are in contact with the substrate, with Phe340 positioned to stabilize Hyp through a proline-aromatic interaction, which is characteristically similar to a cation-π interaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Phe340 is positioned to stabilize Hyp through a proline-aromatic interaction.
source: In HypD, Phe152, Trp277, and Phe340 are in contact with the substrate, with Phe340 positioned to stabilize Hyp through a proline-aromatic interaction, which is characteristically similar to a cation-π interaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Proline-aromatic interactions are characteristically similar to cation-π interactions.
source: In HypD, Phe152, Trp277, and Phe340 are in contact with the substrate, with Phe340 positioned to stabilize Hyp through a proline-aromatic interaction, which is characteristically similar to a cation-π interaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is established knowledge about proline-aromatic interactions.

claim: Energetically favorable interactions occur between proline and aromatic residues within proteins.
source: Previous studies have shown that energetically favorable interactions occur between proline and aromatic residues within proteins (Zondlo, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Favorable proline-aromatic interactions are thought to be due to hydrophobic effects and the interaction of the π face of the aromatic ring with the polarized, partially positively charged C–H bonds of the prolyl ring.
source: These favorable interactions are thought to be due to hydrophobic effects and the interaction of the π face of the aromatic ring with the polarized, partially positively charged C–H bonds of the prolyl ring (Zondlo, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Gly765 forms the glycyl radical species in HypD.
source: We first confirmed that Gly765 forms the glycyl radical species and that Cys434 is catalytically essential by constructing HypD variants containing G765A and C434S substitutions.
evidence: This is confirmed by EPR spectroscopy showing no radical formation in G765A variant (Table 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Cys434 is catalytically essential in HypD.
source: We first confirmed that Gly765 forms the glycyl radical species and that Cys434 is catalytically essential by constructing HypD variants containing G765A and C434S substitutions.
evidence: This is confirmed by activity assays showing no activity in C434S variant (Figure 5A–C).

claim: EPR spectroscopy showed no Gly radical formation for the G765A variant.
source: As expected, EPR spectroscopy showed no Gly radical formation for the G765A variant (Table 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C434A variant can be activated by HypD-AE.
source: Although the C434A variant can be activated by HypD-AE (Table 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), it had no detectable Hyp dehydration activity in our endpoint assay (Figure 5A–C), supporting an essential role for Cys434 in catalysis.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C434A variant had no detectable Hyp dehydration activity.
source: Although the C434A variant can be activated by HypD-AE (Table 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), it had no detectable Hyp dehydration activity in our endpoint assay (Figure 5A–C), supporting an essential role for Cys434 in catalysis.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: The D278N variant lacked Hyp dehydration activity.
source: The D278N variant lacked Hyp dehydration activity, supporting a crucial role for Asp278 in catalysis (Figure 5B–C, Table 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5B–C and Table 2.

claim: Asp278 plays a crucial role in catalysis.
source: The D278N variant lacked Hyp dehydration activity, supporting a crucial role for Asp278 in catalysis (Figure 5B–C, Table 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of activity in the D278N variant.

claim: Asp278 could deprotonate the amino group of zwitterionic Hyp and protonate the departing hydroxyl group.
source: The close proximity of Asp278 to both the amino (3.1 Å) and hydroxyl (3.5 Å) moieties of Hyp suggests that this residue could both deprotonate the amino group of zwitterionic Hyp and protonate the departing hydroxyl group (Figure 4A,E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A,E.

claim: E436Q and H160Q variants lacked Hyp dehydration activity.
source: Additionally, E436Q and H160Q variants lacked Hyp dehydration activity in an endpoint assay, confirming that these residues are also essential (Figure 5B–C, Table 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5B–C and Table 2.

claim: Glu436 and His160 are essential for HypD activity.
source: Additionally, E436Q and H160Q variants lacked Hyp dehydration activity in an endpoint assay, confirming that these residues are also essential (Figure 5B–C, Table 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of activity in the E436Q and H160Q variants.

claim: His160 is positioned 2.5 Å from Glu436.
source: Because of the close proximity of Glu436 to His160 (2.5 Å) (Figure 4A), we propose that His160 tunes the protonation state of Glu436, potentially allowing it to be a hydrogen bond acceptor of the hydroxyl group of Hyp (2.7 Å) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a measurement from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: His160 tunes the protonation state of Glu436.
source: Because of the close proximity of Glu436 to His160 (2.5 Å) (Figure 4A), we propose that His160 tunes the protonation state of Glu436, potentially allowing it to be a hydrogen bond acceptor of the hydroxyl group of Hyp (2.7 Å) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the crystal structure.

claim: The D339N HypD variant lacked Hyp dehydration activity.
source: Strikingly, the D339N HypD variant also lacked Hyp dehydration activity (Figure 5B–C, Table 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5B–C and Table 2.

claim: Asp339 is 6.3 Å from the HypD active site in the Hyp-bound structure.
source: The lack of activity in this variant is particularly surprising because of its distance from the HypD active site (6.3 Å in the Hyp-bound structure, Figure 4A; 7 Å in the glycerol-bound structure, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a measurement from the crystal structure shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Asp339 is absolutely conserved among HypD sequences.
source: However, the biochemical data and the absolute conservation of Asp339 among HypD sequences support a critical role for this residue.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and biochemical data.

claim: His160, Asp278, Asp339, and Glu436 are part of an extensive hydrogen-bonding network surrounding the hydroxyl and amino groups of Hyp and the conserved water molecule.
source: The residues predicted to mediate acid-base chemistry (His160, Asp278, Asp339, Glu436) are part of an extensive hydrogen-bonding network surrounding the hydroxyl and amino groups of Hyp and the conserved water molecule (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 4D–E.

claim: The hydrogen-bonding network provides a plausible route for the proton transfer required to reset the protonation states of active site residues for subsequent rounds of turnover.
source: This network provides a plausible route for the proton transfer required to reset the protonation states of active site residues for subsequent rounds of turnover.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the structural network.

claim: A similar hydrogen-bonding network was reported in CutC.
source: Notably, the presence of a similar network was also reported in CutC (Bodea et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the CutC structure.

claim: HypD-F340A was activated by HypD-AE.
source: Interestingly, although HypD-F340A was activated by HypD-AE (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), it displayed no catalytic activity (Figure 5B–C, Table 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HypD-F340A displayed no catalytic activity.
source: Interestingly, although HypD-F340A was activated by HypD-AE (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), it displayed no catalytic activity (Figure 5B–C, Table 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5B–C and Table 2.

claim: A proline-aromatic interaction with Phe340 is important for Hyp binding.
source: This result provides support for the proposal that a proline-aromatic interaction with Phe340 is important for Hyp binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of activity in the F340A variant.

claim: No activity was observed in the S334A variant.
source: Strikingly, these three variants had different effects on activity. No activity was observed in the S334A variant, indicating this amino acid is essential, likely because of a role in substrate binding/positioning and/or product release.
evidence: This is experimental data from activity assays.

claim: Ser334 is essential for HypD activity.
source: Strikingly, these three variants had different effects on activity. No activity was observed in the S334A variant, indicating this amino acid is essential, likely because of a role in substrate binding/positioning and/or product release.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of activity in the S334A variant.

claim: HypD-Y450F and HypD-T645A exhibited drastically reduced activity.
source: In contrast, HypD-Y450F and HypD-T645A exhibited drastically reduced activity (Figure 5B–C, Table 2), suggesting that they may participate in important interactions but are not essential.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5B–C and Table 2.

claim: The catalytic efficiencies for HypD-Y450F and HypD-T645A were 2–3 orders of magnitude lower than that of wildtype HypD.
source: The catalytic efficiencies for each HypD variant were 2–3 orders of magnitude lower than that of wildtype HypD due to increased Km and decreased kcat values (Table 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Table 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: HypD-Y450F/T645A was activated by HypD-AE.
source: HypD-Y450F/T645A was activated by HypD-AE as detected by EPR spectroscopy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) but showed no detectable activity in the endpoint assay (Figure 5B–C, Table 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HypD-Y450F/T645A showed no detectable activity in the endpoint assay.
source: HypD-Y450F/T645A was activated by HypD-AE as detected by EPR spectroscopy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) but showed no detectable activity in the endpoint assay (Figure 5B–C, Table 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5B–C and Table 2.

claim: Little deuterium incorporation in product (~10%) was observed when the HypD coupled assay was performed in D2O using unlabeled Hyp.
source: Remarkably, we observed little deuterium incorporation in product (~10% based on the assay run in triplicate and compared to a control of Pro dissolved in D2O) (Figure 6C, see Figure 6—source data 1 for relevant MS/MS transitions).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Solvent accessibility of Cys434 is not a major issue during catalysis.
source: These data indicate that solvent accessibility of Cys434 is not a major issue and that if P5C ring-opening/tautomerization is occurring, it is not happening quickly enough to have a substantial impact on P5C hydrogen/deuterium exchange.
evidence: This is inferred from the deuterium labeling experiment results.

claim: Formation of [2,4,5-D3]-L-proline was observed when the HypD coupled assay was performed with 2,5,5-D3-Hyp as the substrate.
source: We next performed the HypD coupled assay with 2,5,5-D3-Hyp as the substrate, and formation of [2,4,5-D3]-L-proline was observed, characterized by high-resolution MS, LC-MS/MS and 1H, 13C, 1H-1H COrrelated SpectroscopY (COSY), and 1H-13C heteronuclear single quantum coherence (1H-13C HSQC) NMR experiments (Figure 6D–E, Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 6D–E and Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: A shift of a deuterium atom from C5 to C4 was observed in the HypD reaction.
source: Thus, we observe a shift of a deuterium atom from C5 to C4, which is consistent with C5 being the site of hydrogen-atom abstraction and C4 being the site of hydrogen-atom re-abstraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the deuterium labeling experiment results.

claim: C5 is the site of hydrogen-atom abstraction in the HypD reaction.
source: Thus, we observe a shift of a deuterium atom from C5 to C4, which is consistent with C5 being the site of hydrogen-atom abstraction and C4 being the site of hydrogen-atom re-abstraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the deuterium labeling experiment results.

claim: C4 is the site of hydrogen-atom re-abstraction in the HypD reaction.
source: Thus, we observe a shift of a deuterium atom from C5 to C4, which is consistent with C5 being the site of hydrogen-atom abstraction and C4 being the site of hydrogen-atom re-abstraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the deuterium labeling experiment results.

claim: Direct elimination is the mechanism used by GRE eliminases.
source: Experimental and computational investigations have provided strong support for direct elimination as the mechanism used by GRE eliminases (Feliks and Ullmann, 2012; Kovačević et al., 2018; Levin and Balskus, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hyp binds as a zwitterion in the active site based on its protonation state at neutral pH.
source: After activation of HypD by HypD-AE, we predict that Hyp binds as a zwitterion in the active site based on its protonation state at neutral pH (Figure 7, step I).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on chemical knowledge and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cys434 abstracts the pro-S hydrogen atom of C5 of Hyp.
source: In particular, the structure suggests that Cys434 abstracts the pro-S hydrogen atom of C5, which is the closest to Cys434 (2.6 Å) (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Hydrogen atom abstraction of the pro-S instead of the pro-R hydrogen atom is consistent with the stereochemistry determined for the reaction catalyzed by PFL.
source: Hydrogen atom abstraction of the pro-S instead of the pro-R hydrogen atom is consistent with the stereochemistry determined for the reaction catalyzed by PFL (Frey et al., 1994) and that is proposed for most other GRE eliminases based on structural data (O'Brien et al., 2004; LaMattina et al., 2016; Xing et al., 2019; Bodea et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on other GREs.

claim: Deprotonation of the Hyp amino group occurs before hydrogen atom abstraction from C5.
source: Since the initial hydrogen atom abstraction steps in GRE-catalyzed transformations have high activation energy barriers (Feliks and Ullmann, 2012; Liu et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2019), we propose that deprotonation of the Hyp amino group occurs first, as the lone pair of a free amino group could stabilize the radical forming on C5 through conjugative electron delocalization (Figure 7, step I to II) (Viehe et al., 1985).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on computational studies and chemical principles, shown in Figure 7.

claim: The lone pair of a free amino group could stabilize the radical forming on C5 through conjugative electron delocalization.
source: Since the initial hydrogen atom abstraction steps in GRE-catalyzed transformations have high activation energy barriers (Feliks and Ullmann, 2012; Liu et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2019), we propose that deprotonation of the Hyp amino group occurs first, as the lone pair of a free amino group could stabilize the radical forming on C5 through conjugative electron delocalization (Figure 7, step I to II) (Viehe et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on radical stabilization.

claim: Asp278 is positioned appropriately to act as the catalytic base that deprotonates the amino group.
source: The structure suggests that Asp278 is positioned appropriately to act as the catalytic base that deprotonates the amino group (Figure 7, step I).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 7.

claim: Hydrogen atom abstraction from C5 of Hyp results in an α-aminoalkyl radical intermediate.
source: Hydrogen atom abstraction from C5 of Hyp results in an α-aminoalkyl radical intermediate (Figure 7, step II to III).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal shown in Figure 7.

claim: HypD presents a unique case where an α-aminoalkyl radical intermediate forms in the absence of an adjacent carboxyl group.
source: Although Cα-centered radicals of amino acids are stabilized by delocalization of the unpaired electron onto adjacent amino and carboxyl groups (the captodative effect) (Viehe et al., 1985), HypD presents a unique case where an α-aminoalkyl radical intermediate forms in the absence of an adjacent carboxyl group.
evidence: This is a mechanistic observation based on the structure of Hyp.

claim: α-Aminoalkyl radicals are often generated as reactive intermediates to drive substitution reactions in organic chemistry.
source: Although rarely reported in enzymatic chemistry, α-aminoalkyl radicals are often generated as reactive intermediates to drive substitution reactions in organic chemistry (Renaud and Giraud, 1996; Nakajima et al., 2016; Mondal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to organic chemistry literature.

claim: Rapid elimination of the hydroxyl leaving group from the α-aminoalkyl radical intermediate is facilitated by protonation of the departing hydroxyl group by a catalytic acid.
source: We propose that rapid elimination of the hydroxyl leaving group from this intermediate occurs and is facilitated by protonation of the departing hydroxyl group by a catalytic acid (Figure 7, step IV to V).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal shown in Figure 7.

claim: The catalytic acid that protonates the departing hydroxyl group is Asp278.
source: Based on the structure and mutagenesis, we propose that the catalytic acid is Asp278, the same residue that likely deprotonates the Hyp amino group, which would reset Asp278's protonation state (Figure 7, step II to IV).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the crystal structure and mutagenesis data, shown in Figure 7.

claim: The elimination of the hydroxyl group of Hyp generates a double bond, resulting in the generation of an enamine radical cation intermediate.
source: The elimination of the hydroxyl group of Hyp generates a double bond, resulting in the generation of an enamine radical cation intermediate (Figure 7, step V).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal shown in Figure 7.

claim: The final radical transfer from P5C to Cys434 occurs at C4.
source: Because the HypD coupled assay with 2,5,5-D3-Hyp resulted in formation of 2,4,5-D3-Pro (Figure 6D–E), suggesting that the initial deuterium atom abstracted from C5 by Cys434 is transferred back to C4, we propose that the final radical transfer from P5C to Cys434 occurs at C4 (Figure 7, step VII).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on deuterium labeling experiments shown in Figure 6D–E and Figure 7.

claim: Formation of the double bond settles the Hyp's Cγ-exo pucker into a nearly planar pyrroline species.
source: This proposal also makes sense from a structural perspective. Formation of this double bond settles the Hyp's Cγ-exo pucker into a nearly planar pyrroline species.
evidence: This is a structural inference based on chemical knowledge.

claim: Modeling suggests that C4 of P5C is closer to Cys434 than is C5.
source: Manual docking of the product P5C into the active site (Figure 8B) allows us to approximate how this change in ring puckering should affect the relative proximities of substrate/product atoms to the thiyl radical-forming Cys434 (Figure 8). Specifically, modeling suggests that C4 of P5C is closer to Cys434 than is C5 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is based on molecular modeling shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Asp339 is positioned to serve as the catalytic base via a water-mediated interaction to deprotonate the enamine radical cation intermediate.
source: Hydrogen atom re-abstraction from Cys434 could occur at this point or may follow the deprotonation of an enamine radical cation intermediate (pKa ~5.5–7 Jonsson et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2017), which would be expected to generate a more nucleophilic, α-iminyl radical species (Figure 7, step VI to VII) (Roberts, 1999). Asp339, which we show here is catalytically essential, appears well positioned to serve as the catalytic base via a water-mediated interaction (Figure 7 step VI to VII).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the crystal structure and mutagenesis data, shown in Figure 7.

claim: Asp339 could serve as a catalytic acid in the protonation of the P5C carboxylate.
source: Asp339 could also serve as a catalytic acid in the subsequent protonation of the P5C carboxylate (Figure 7, step VII to VIII).
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal shown in Figure 7.

claim: Protonation of the P5C carboxylate should aid in its release.
source: Protonation of the P5C carboxylate should aid in its release as the very close interaction with the P5C carboxyl group and Ser334 (2.5 Å) would be unfavorable if the carboxyl moiety were protonated.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on structural considerations.

claim: The final mechanistic step is reformation of the glycyl radical species on HypD and product release.
source: The final mechanistic step is reformation of the glycyl radical species on HypD (Figure 7, step VIII) and product release.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal shown in Figure 7.

claim: The structural and biochemical data allow identification of a key set of HypD residues important for catalysis and substrate binding.
source: Importantly, these structural and biochemical data have allowed us to identify a key set of HypD residues important for catalysis and substrate binding, leading to a deeper understanding of how this prominent human gut bacterial enzyme performs difficult radical chemistry.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the manuscript.

claim: The data will inform drug design efforts directed toward C. difficile HypD.
source: Not only will these data inform drug design efforts directed toward C. difficile HypD, they should also allow us to more accurately identify other pathogens that contain HypD enzymes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications of the work.

claim: The data should allow more accurate identification of other pathogens that contain HypD enzymes.
source: Not only will these data inform drug design efforts directed toward C. difficile HypD, they should also allow us to more accurately identify other pathogens that contain HypD enzymes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications of the work.

claim: Hyp dehydration is an exciting transformation that is unique among GREs and more broadly among enzymes.
source: The Hyp dehydration is an exciting transformation that is unique among GREs and more broadly among enzymes.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the novelty of the reaction.

claim: The manuscript proposes the first mechanism for chemical reversal of proline hydroxylation.
source: Herein we propose the first mechanism for chemical reversal of one of the most common post-translational modifications, proline hydroxylation.
evidence: This is a summary of the novel contribution of the work.

claim: Through HypD, gut microbes have found a way to opportunistically profit from the abundant yet catabolically underutilized metabolite Hyp.
source: Through HypD, gut microbes have found a way to opportunistically profit from the abundant yet catabolically underutilized metabolite Hyp.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the biological significance of HypD.
